LEARN WITH DAYFINDER

Date calculation guides

Short explanations of the rules behind the tools, with practical examples.

How weekdays are calculated

DayFinder converts a valid date into a day count and maps the remainder after division by seven to Sunday through Saturday. The tool uses the proleptic Gregorian calendar consistently from 1583 onward.

Example: 15 August 1947 was a Friday.

The Gregorian leap-year rule

A year is a leap year when it is divisible by 4, except century years must also be divisible by 400. Therefore 2000 was a leap year, while 1900 and 2100 are not.

Counting working days

Choose a date range and weekend pattern. The calculator examines each date, excludes weekends, then excludes selected fixed-date and custom holidays. Always enter the current official holiday list for payroll, banking, legal or contractual work.

ISO week numbers

ISO 8601 weeks start on Monday. Week 1 is the week containing the year’s first Thursday. This means some late-December dates belong to week 1 of the next ISO year, and some early-January dates belong to the previous ISO year.

Exact age

Exact age is reported as completed years, then completed months, then remaining days. It is more informative than simply dividing the total number of days by 365.

Historical-date caution

Different countries adopted the Gregorian calendar in different years. DayFinder applies Gregorian rules backward consistently from 1583. Researchers should verify the historical calendar used in the place and period they are studying.
